Does adding to a winner help? — the rule tested, not asserted

Correction — I had this backwards. An earlier build of this report said adding to MCD would have turned a +1.48R winner into a +0.23R scratch. That number came from a bug, not from the market: the add was being evaluated before the stop check on the same bar, so an add made late in the 09-23 session retro-actively raised a stop that price had already taken out earlier that morning. With the bar processed in the correct order, adding is better, not worse.

The adopted rule is the top row, and it wins by $25. 0.00R with 2 adds returns +5.79R; the +0.50R gate with the same two adds returns +5.74R. The difference is +0.05R — one AAPL add — on a twelve-position sample. Picking the argmax off a surface this flat is curve-fitting, and the cost shows up immediately: a +0.00R gate will add to a position that is up 0.09R, which is not adding to strength, it is just buying more. The rule is adopted as asked, with every risk guard left in front of it.
And it breaches the risk cap. Simulated forward, the adopted rule carries $4,100 of open heat — 8.2% — and with this week's two new shorts that is 10.2%, through the 10% ceiling and well through the 8.5% event-week ceiling. NKE reaches 412 shares three sessions before it reports. The extra R is not free; it is bought with size, and the caps below are what stop that size arriving all at once.

Seven adds in a one-way tape is not proof. Every one was made into a position that kept going, in a month where the average stock fell while the index did not. That is evidence the rule behaves correctly in a trend — not evidence it is safe in a choppy one, where the raised stop is exactly what gets hit. The live book below is not rewritten: no report ever published an add, so none was taken, and every position you hold is single size. The rule applies from next week.

What has actually been learned

The trailing stop was the missing piece, and it was expensive. Three things were wrong at once: a live position's stop was being replaced weekly by a fresh setup's stop instead of trailed from its own fill; the stop only moved once a week, so a position could drift for five sessions; and T1 closed the whole trade. Fixing all three moves the record from -1.22R of closed losses with everything else unbooked to 1.01R realised with two runners still working. CPRT is the clearest example of the cost: at +0.75R it was carrying $876 of open risk, 1.75× its original position risk, because price had run in our favour and the stop never followed.

The stop now moves every session, not every report. LOW's stop has ratcheted eleven times since 09-09, from 209.93 down to 197.89. MCD's has moved thirteen times. Every open card carries the arithmetic so you can do it yourself on any evening the market gives you a new bar — the weekly report is a checkpoint, not the only time the stop is allowed to move.

Adding to a winner is worth more than this report previously claimed, and the rule is now adopted at the setting that maximises R. Last week's build said an add to MCD would have cost 1.25R. That was a bug in bar processing, not a market result. Re-run correctly and swept across both the threshold and the number of adds allowed, the best setting — add from +0.00R, up to two adds — produces +5.79R against +3.83R for trail-only across the same twelve positions, and none of the seven adds ever came within 0.26R of its raised stop. It is adopted from next week, behind an earnings block, the breadth rule and the heat cap. It beats a +0.50R gate by 0.05R, which is one AAPL add and $25 — so the honest reading is that the benefit comes from adding at all, not from where exactly the threshold sits. The caveat is real though: four adds in a one-way tape is not proof, and the mechanism that makes an add pay in a trend — a tighter stop on a bigger position — is the same one that makes it expensive in a chop.

Two positions had gone missing from the book. BIIB was planned on 09-11, dropped from the 09-18 report, and triggered on 09/22 — live for four sessions with no card. The selection step is now a union with the open book and the build fails outright if any open position has no card.

Twelve positions is still not evidence of edge. Four weeks, two closed trades, two runners, and a tape where the average stock fell while the index did not. A short book will look good in this market whether or not the selection rules add anything. The honest claim stays narrow: the rules execute as specified and the risk controls now bind where they should. Ask again after a quarter, and especially after an up-week.

The logic, stated as rules

Every filter below is computed from split-adjusted daily OHLCV — nothing is discretionary, and nothing was chosen after seeing which names would pass. The rule set fuses four published frameworks: Weinstein's stage analysis for the regime a stock is in, Minervini's trend template for whether it is in a genuine Stage 2 advance, the Donchian / Turtle channel breakout for the trigger, and volatility contraction plus volume signature for whether the base is being accumulated or merely drifting.

Long — Stage 2 trend template (all seven must be true)

  1. Moving-average stack. Close > 50 SMA > 150 SMA > 200 SMA, and close above all three.
  2. Slope. 200 SMA higher than 21 sessions ago and 50 SMA higher than 10 sessions ago — the trend is being renewed, not decaying.
  3. Proximity to high. Within 25% of the 52-week high. Leadership does not hide in the bottom of its range.
  4. Distance from low. At least 25% above the 52-week low — filters out dead-cat bounces off a Stage 4 base.
  5. Relative strength. RS in the top 30% of the universe, where RS is the IBD-style weighted excess return over SPY: 40% × 3-month, 20% each × 6-, 9- and 12-month.
  6. Liquidity. 20-day average dollar volume ≥ $50M, so a 10–40 share-lot or a spread fills without slippage.
  7. Base structure. Range depth ≤ 18% measured over the shortest of the last 25, 40 or 60 sessions that qualifies.

Long — setup trigger (base rules plus these)

  • Proximity to pivot. Price within 7% of the base high — close enough that a buy stop is a trade, not a hope.
  • Not extended. No more than 14% above the 50 SMA. A stock already 3–5 ATR extended is a bad breakout buy regardless of how good the trend looks.
  • Volatility contraction or accumulation. Either ATR% today ≤ its level 20 sessions ago, or ATR% ≤ 0.85× its level 40 sessions ago (the VCP signature); or up-volume ÷ down-volume over 20 sessions ≥ 0.95.

Short — Stage 4 breakdown (all six must be true)

  1. Inverted stack. Close below both the 50 SMA and 200 SMA, and 50 SMA below 200 SMA.
  2. Slope. 200 SMA or 50 SMA declining — supply is in control on at least one timeframe.
  3. Proximity to low. No more than 25% above the 52-week low.
  4. Damage done. At least 18% below the 52-week high — this is a broken stock, not a pullback in an uptrend.
  5. Relative weakness. RS in the bottom 30% of the universe.
  6. Distribution. Up-volume ÷ down-volume over 20 sessions ≤ 1.05 — rallies are not being bought.

Trigger adds: price within 7% above the 25/40/60-session base low, and not more than 14% below the 50 SMA (an already-collapsed stock mean-reverts violently and is a poor short entry).

Entry, stop and target construction

  • Entry. Stop order at the structural pivot — the higher of the base high and the 20-day Donchian high for longs, the lower of the base low and the 20-day Donchian low for shorts — plus a 0.10 ATR buffer through the level. No anticipation, no limit orders inside the base.
  • Stop. The wider of the nearest structural level (10-day extreme, base extreme, or nearest clustered S/R zone) offset by 0.30 ATR, capped at 2.2 ATR from entry. The Turtle system's 2N stop, with structure allowed to tighten it but never to widen it past 2.2N.
  • Target 1. Entry ± 1.5R. Take a third to a half off; move the stop to breakeven.
  • Target 2. The measured move — base height projected from the pivot — or 2.8R, whichever is further.
  • Trail. Once a position is on it is managed by this report every week, and the stop ratchets one way only. Each week the managed stop is the tightest of: the stop already in force; the 5-day Donchian extreme in the opposite direction offset by 0.25 ATR (horizon-matched to a 3–15 day swing, where the Turtle 20-day exit is far too loose); the price that caps remaining give-back at 1R; and the original fill once the trade is +1.0R or better. It is then floored 0.75 ATR away from the last close so it never sits inside the noise band. A re-issued stop can tighten risk on a live trade but can never widen it.
  • Sizing. Shares = $500 ÷ (entry − stop), capped at 30% of account notional per position.
  • Book heat. Total risk across every position — open, added-to and new — is capped at 15% of the account, cut to 13.5% in any week where a live position reports earnings inside the holding window. Heat is spent in a fixed order: positions flagged to cut are closed first and their risk freed, open positions keep theirs, then adds, then new entries in score order. Anything that does not fit is deferred with its levels intact, not deleted.

How open positions are tracked

  • One position per symbol and side. The first plan to trigger opens the position. Every later week's plan for the same symbol and side is a management update — a revised stop and revised targets on the trade already on — not a second trade. Grading each week's plan file as an independent cohort double-counts every carried position, and that is exactly what the earlier scorecards in this series did.
  • Selection is a union, never a filter. The weekly book is this week's screen picks plus every still-open position. The sector cap, the breadth rule and the setup-ready filter govern new entries only. None of them may drop a live position out of the book, because the result is a real position running with a stale stop that nobody is watching. The build fails if any open position lacks a card.
  • Re-entry is allowed, repetition is not. Once a position closes the symbol goes flat, and only a plan issued after the close date may open a new one — so the book never re-enters on the same stale level twice.
  • T1 takes half off, it does not close the position. Half comes off at Target 1 and books 0.75R; the balance rides the same daily trail toward Target 2 with its stop moved to at least breakeven. Booking the whole position at T1 caps every winner at exactly 1.5R while every loser is free to run to −1R, and the trail is what is supposed to pay for the losers.
  • Adding to a position that is working. A position is added to when this week's plan re-issues the same side at a trigger beyond the fill and the position is already through the gate. Half a unit per add, at most two per position. After an add the stop on the whole position moves so combined open risk stays at 1R of the original unit — an add can never turn a winner into more than a 1R loser. Never add back after Target 1 has been taken: scaling out and buying back in are two decisions that cancel, with two lots of slippage.
  • What blocks an add. Four separate guards, any one of which is enough: the name reports earnings inside the holding window; breadth is below 40% and the add is on the long side, because adding shares to a long is owning more long exposure and the no-new-longs rule covers it; the name no longer passes its side of the screen; or the add does not fit under the book heat cap. Heat is spent in a fixed order — positions flagged to cut are closed first and their risk freed, open positions keep theirs, then adds, then new entries in score order. Anything that does not fit is deferred with its levels intact, not deleted.
  • Why adds rank ahead of new entries. Adding to a position that is already working is a higher-probability use of the same risk than a fresh trigger that may never fill — roughly a third of planned triggers never do.

How the levels on each chart were derived

  • Swing highs / lows. Fractal pivots — a bar whose high is the strict maximum (or low the strict minimum) of the five bars either side of it. Marked ▼ and ▲ on the charts.
  • Support / resistance zones. Three-bar fractal pivots from the last 15 months, clustered where they fall within 0.6 ATR of each other. Each zone carries a touch count and the date it was last tested — a level touched four times is a different object from one touched once.
  • Volume profile. Six months of daily bars, 80 price bins, each bar's volume distributed uniformly across its high–low range. POC is the highest-volume bin; the value area is the 70% of volume around it; HVN are local maxima above the 75th percentile (shaded purple — price tends to stall and rotate there); LVN are local minima below the 25th percentile (grey dotted — price tends to move through them quickly).
  • Donchian channels. 20-day and 55-day extremes, excluding the current bar.

Sources

Minervini trend template criteria — Deepvue, TraderLion on stage analysis. Donchian breakout lengths, the N/ATR volatility unit, 2N stop and 20-day trailing exit — the original Turtle trading rules. Volume-profile HVN/LVN/POC methodology — AlgoVistra, FXOpen on fixed-range volume profile. Price data via Yahoo Finance; live quotes, option chains, Greeks and the earnings calendar via the connected brokerage MCP.

What the leadership is telling you

The short list has stopped being a consumer story. Twenty-five names are setup-ready shorts this week across nine sectors. The top of the list is still consumer discretionary — HD at 95.3, LOW at 95.0, MCD at 94.9, PDD at 94.0 — but utilities (EXC 91.7, NEE 91.5), communication services (NFLX 90.5, CMCSA 89.7), industrials (VRSK 90.3, UPS 79.4) and information technology (IBM 88.8, ADBE 83.6, ADSK 87.0) are all now represented with scores above 79. A breakdown screen that spans nine sectors while the index sits 1% off its high is the clearest internal warning this report has produced.

The long side has narrowed to health care and one megacap. Twelve names are setup-ready longs. BIIB (83.9), JNJ, GILD, MRK, VRTX and DXCM are all health care; AAPL is the only technology name; MET is the only financial. The semiconductor complex — AMD, MU, INTC, MRVL — passes the trend template but every one of them is 15–25% above its 50-day, which is exactly the extension the setup filter exists to refuse.

Utilities are the group to watch, and not for the reason you would expect. EXC and NEE both score above 91 as shorts. This report refused both, because the one utility short already on the book — CEG — is the only losing position in it at −0.63R. A sector thesis that is not working in the position you already have is not a thesis to double.

Why some high scorers were not given plans

Four filters sit on top of the raw ranking this week. Book heat — the ten open positions already carry $4,100 of risk (8.2% of the account) against a 10% cap, which left room for two new entries and no more, so the short list was cut at two regardless of how many names qualified. Sector concentration — the two-per-sector cap counts open positions, and consumer discretionary is already at three (NKE, LOW, MCD), which is why HD at 95.3 and PDD at 94.0 — the first and fourth highest scores on the entire board — were both refused. Sector confirmation — a second short is not opened in a sector where the existing short is underwater, which removed EXC (91.7) and NEE (91.5) because CEG is at −0.63R. Setup-ready only — CHTR (98.4) and TTD (97.2) are the two highest short scores in the universe and neither is setup-ready; both sit more than 16% below their 50-day averages, where a mean-reversion squeeze is the most likely next move.

What survived was NFLX (90.5, communication services, no existing position) and VRSK (90.3, industrials, where CPRT is +0.75R and confirming). Neither is the top-scoring name available. Both are the top-scoring names that the risk rules permit, which is a different and better thing.

Also corrected: MCD reached Target 1 too. The 09-23 session opened at 250.29 and closed at 238.32 — a 16-point range that took out T1 at 239.14. Half came off there for +0.68R booked. The balance is short from 254.39 with the stop trailed to 247.70, locking +0.60R, for +1.48R in total. On the merits it is still the most distributive name in the universe: 30.8% off the high, 1.1% above the 52-week low, up/down volume 0.17. On the question of adding: the 09-18 re-issue published a 247.22 trigger, only 0.64R beyond the 254.39 fill. The pyramid rule requires an add to sit at least 1R beyond the fill, so it does not qualify — and testing it the other way is instructive. Forcing the add through raises the average to 252.00, pulls the combined stop up to 249.52 to keep total risk at 1R, and the 09-23 bar prints a 250.32 high before it collapses. The add would have turned a +1.48R winner into a +0.23R scratch and forfeited the entire 16-point day. Do not add.

New, and the only new entry in the report with a usable option market. Netflix is 43.0% below its 52-week high, RS in the 6.5th percentile, up/down volume 0.35, and only 5.8% below its 50-day — the least extended of any short scoring above 90, which is what keeps the stop at 2.13 ATR rather than the 2.20 cap. Communication services is a genuinely new sector for this book. Option liquidity is the best in the report by a distance: 18,284 contracts open on the 70 put, 25,276 on the 65, and a 2.8% spread on the long leg. This week's decisions, in order

  • 1. Close ABBV. It fails the trend template this week. The entry thesis has stopped being true, which is a cleaner reason to exit than the −0.26R — and it frees $181 of heat.
  • 2. Close or sharply reduce CEG. −0.63R, short score down from 89 to 71.8, up/down volume back to 0.84, stop only 2.2% away. Its trail has never moved once — the ratchet has had nothing to work with, which is itself the signal. Frees $182.
  • 3. Add to CPRT, CSGP and LOW. 128 shares at 27.44, 88 at 27.16, 22 at 186.69. Each is half a unit; each moves the stop on the whole position afterwards so combined risk stays at 1R. Full numbers on the cards.
  • 4. Leave the runners alone. MCD and PEP have each booked half at T1 and have both already taken their two adds. Do not add back, do not take the rest off early. Their stops at 247.70 and 132.87 lock +0.38R and +0.64R on the balance.
  • 5. Move every other open stop to the "stop for Monday" figure on its card, then keep moving it each evening using the worksheet on the same card.
  • 6. Place the two new shorts. NFLX 69.90 sell stop, VRSK 166.91 sell stop.

It is why no third add was allowed on it and why the cap is at 13.5% rather than 15% this week. Decide before Monday whether you are flat, hedged, or accepting it.
  • ⚠ PEP reports 2026-10-08, eight trading days in, on the 70-share runner.
  • No adds on the long side. AAPL and BIIB both clear the add gate on merit and are refused by the breadth rule — adding shares to a long is owning more long exposure, and breadth is at 37.3%.

Execution notes

  • Monday 2026-09-28 is the next session — a normal week. If a stock gaps through its trigger by more than 0.5 ATR, stand aside rather than chasing; the reward:risk the plan was built on no longer exists.
  • The option expiry is 2026-11-20, 53 DTE. The 35–45 band points at the 2026-11-06 weekly, but the November monthly is where the open interest is. Longer expiry means slower theta — the NFLX structure is within a cent of theta-neutral, which is the point.
  • Only one of the twelve cards has a tradeable option structure. NFLX. VRSK has no fillable market at any expiry, and the ten open positions are management cards where the actionable number is the stop, not a new spread.
  • Options are for the trend, not the trigger. If the NFLX short stops out in the first week you lose roughly the delta-adjusted amount shown on the card (≈$388), not the full $1,045 debit. That is the basis the five contracts were sized on. If you cannot honour the stop, trade shares.
  • Confirm the breakdown on volume. A trigger that fires on below-average volume is a lower-quality signal. A breakdown day below 1.2× the 50-day average volume deserves a half-size entry.
  • Re-run the scan on any 2%+ index day. Base depths, Donchian levels and the pivot itself move; a plan built on Friday's close is stale after a large directional session.
  • The stop ratchet is one-way. If a revised stop on a card looks wider than what you already have working, keep yours. The report never widens risk on a live position, and neither should you.

What would invalidate this whole report

The risk has been on the same side for three weeks and it is getting more crowded. With breadth at 37.3% and a book that is seven-tenths short, the dangerous scenario is not a further decline — it is a reversal. Readings this depressed are where violent counter-trend rallies start, and the most beaten-down names squeeze hardest. A breadth thrust back through 45%, or SPY making a new high on expanding participation, would hurt this book badly and fast.

The specific tell: NKE, LOW, MCD and PEP are all within 1.6% of their 52-week lows. If they stop making new lows while SPY holds, the trade is finished regardless of what the scores say. A second tell is the one already visible — CEG bounced 3% off its low and immediately became the worst position in the book.

The other invalidation is unchanged: VIX above 22 with SPY below its 50-day (761.57, -1.27% from Friday's close). That is a regime where everything correlates to one and position sizing matters more than selection.
